records.recommendation: Review whether this unit should move to Schlüchtern and be renamed, and whether it still counts as a gas plant.

The plant is planned at 276 MW, with 80 percent from fuel cells and 20 percent from gas burning, and hydrogen from the mid 2030s. About 50 MW of heat would go to a district heating network. GEM's 135 MW estimate was based on gas supplying half of 250 to 270 MW, so it no longer matches. Gas would supply roughly 55 MW if the 20 percent applies to the 276 MW. I did not change the capacity because the source does not give a gas capacity.

records.plant_name: Mukran FSRU LNG Terminal power station
records.recommendation: Out of scope. Do not add a plant. The 39.9 MW is the combined engine rating of one LNG ship, and the shore-side power plant that was once planned has been dropped.
records.researcher_notes: The possible-updates row says 39.9 MW from the generators on board the Neptune, one of two floating LNG import ships at Mukran on Rügen, run by Deutsche ReGas. German Wikipedia lists the Neptune with three Wärtsilä 12V50 DF engines of 11,400 kW each and one 6L50DF engine of 5,700 kW. Together that is about 39.9 MW. This is the ship's own engine rating, not a power plant that sells electricity. The original permit for the terminal included a shore-side combined heat and power plant, which would have supplied heat to Sassnitz. In July 2024 Deutsche ReGas said it would not build it. The Federal Administrative Court ruled in 2025 that dropping it needed a formal permit change. In March 2026 the state environment office in Vorpommern granted that change, so the terminal may run permanently on the ships' own gas generators. A trade press report dated March 20, 2026 confirms this. I found no shore-side generator of any size and no electric export figure. The ship engines run the ship and the regasification. A reviewer should treat this as ship equipment, not a tracked plant. Recheck only if Deutsche ReGas or the town of Sassnitz revives the shore plant.
